science_records.claim: For a one-dimensional motion, displacement is final position minus initial position and distance is total path length.
science_records.law_or_model: signed one-dimensional position and cumulative distance
assumptions: One fixed coordinate axis is declared
A common reference frame for all positions
conditions_and_limits: The absolute value of net displacement never exceeds path length.
A coordinate reversal changes displacement sign but does not alter path distance.
science_records.units_and_signs: x and Δx in m, east positive unless specified; distance is nonnegative.

science_records.claim: For two bodies' velocities measured in the same non-rotating reference frame, relative velocity along one axis is the signed difference.
science_records.law_or_model: v(B/A) = vB − vA; Galilean composition in classical one-dimensional kinematics
assumptions: The compared velocities are signed on the same axis
Speeds sufficiently slow that elementary Galilean composition applies
The frame is suitably inertial for subsequent Newtonian force reasoning
conditions_and_limits: Relative velocities stated in different intermediate frames must be composed in order.
Do not add unsigned speeds automatically or infer meeting time without initial separation.
Individual displacement and path length need not be invariant under a moving frame; simultaneous separation and a meeting event are invariant under a common translation.
science_records.units_and_signs: Signed velocities in m/s, signed east positive.

science_records.claim: On a velocity-time graph, the signed area over a time interval is displacement, whereas total distance sums the magnitudes of segment contributions.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise v–t area and x–t slope
assumptions: The graphed quantities use a fixed coordinate system
Time interval is partitioned at genuine changes of velocity law
conditions_and_limits: Signed area is not automatically positive distance.
Vertical velocity jumps are idealizations; actual finite force implies finite-time change.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; signed area m; positive and negative velocities are directions.

science_records.claim: Each position formula applies only over the interval whose motion conditions define it.
science_records.law_or_model: piecewise constant-velocity motion and interval-filtered intersections
assumptions: Correct start times and initial positions are known
Each interval's velocity law is valid only within declared bounds
conditions_and_limits: A solution outside its interval is inadmissible even if the algebra is correct.
After a stop, reversal or delayed departure, use a new position expression with continuity at the boundary.
science_records.units_and_signs: Global clock t in s; positions m; each segment retains signed velocity m/s.

science_records.claim: Over a time interval, average speed is total path length divided by duration; average signed velocity is net displacement divided by duration.
science_records.law_or_model: averages from path length and signed position
assumptions: One global start and end time
Correct distinction between path length and signed position
conditions_and_limits: Replacing displacement with path length in average velocity is invalid.
An object may have zero average velocity while having nonzero average speed.
science_records.units_and_signs: Speed ≥0, velocity has sign, both measured in m/s; length in metres and duration in seconds.

science_records.claim: For motion split into constant-velocity intervals, total distance is the sum of |v_i| Δt_i and net displacement is the sum of v_i Δt_i.
assumptions: Each stage's signed velocity and interval duration are defined
Each interval is counted once and no time gap is overlooked
conditions_and_limits: The magnitude of net displacement never exceeds total distance.
A reversal makes the algebraic displacement sum differ from summed distance.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; time s; sums produce metres.

science_records.claim: For a straight-line segment on an x–t graph, signed slope Δx/Δt equals the constant velocity in that interval.
science_records.law_or_model: position-time slope and inverse graphical reconstruction
assumptions: Position and time axes have known scale and units
Motion is piecewise constant velocity for straight graph segments
conditions_and_limits: A horizontal x–t segment means rest in that frame, not zero position.
Graph height on x–t is position, whereas graph height on v–t is velocity.
science_records.units_and_signs: Position in m; time s; slope m/s.

science_records.claim: For a fixed straight axis, a uniformly spaced reading r maps to physical position x=b+kr, with nonzero signed scale k. Changing origin or direction changes coordinates, not physical separation.
assumptions: Straight stationary reference axis; uniform scale; both markers refer to the same physical points.
conditions_and_limits: Two distinct calibrated markers determine b and k only under the uniform-scale assumption.
A moving origin requires a time-dependent transformation; nonuniform scales require more information.
science_records.units_and_signs: x in m, r in scale divisions, k in m/division; sign of k gives axis orientation.

science_records.claim: Total path length D is at least |x_f−x_i|; in a straight monotone interval D=|Δx|. For a piecewise monotone route D is the sum of the absolute changes between all actual turns.
science_records.law_or_model: One-dimensional path-length ledger and endpoint lower bound
assumptions: Positions use one fixed metre axis; all stated turning points are included for an exact ledger.
conditions_and_limits: Finite position samples alone generally give only a lower bound.
An exact upper bound cannot be inferred without additional restrictions on unobserved motion.
science_records.units_and_signs: Positions and signed displacement in m; path length D≥0 in m.

science_records.claim: Average acceleration is Δv/Δt; instantaneous acceleration is the slope of v–t. In one dimension, nonzero v and a of the same sign increase speed, opposite signs decrease speed.
assumptions: Fixed one-dimensional axis; elapsed time positive; instantaneous sign criterion applies where velocity is nonzero.
conditions_and_limits: An interval average does not imply constant acceleration.
At a reversal v passes through zero; direction of acceleration is not itself direction of motion.
science_records.units_and_signs: Velocity m/s; acceleration m/s²; east-positive unless declared.

science_records.claim: For constant signed acceleration on an interval, v=u+at, Δx=ut+½at²=½(u+v)t, and v²=u²+2aΔx.
assumptions: Constant acceleration on the stated interval; one fixed coordinate axis; t is elapsed time since interval start.
conditions_and_limits: v² relation loses sign information; recover sign from time/domain.
Displacement is not distance when velocity reverses.
Variable acceleration needs a different model or piecewise intervals.
science_records.units_and_signs: u,v m/s; a m/s²; t s; Δx m.

science_records.claim: For uniform circular motion at radius r and period T, speed is 2πr/T; velocity is tangent and changes direction. Displacement is the endpoint vector, not arc length.
science_records.law_or_model: Uniform circular motion, arc length and vector displacement
assumptions: Fixed circle radius, fixed centre and constant speed; motion in a plane; defined orientation.
conditions_and_limits: Whole-revolution displacement is zero but speed is not.
Average velocity is the vector displacement divided by elapsed time; not the average of speed magnitudes.
Quantitative centripetal acceleration/force is an extension; no force law is needed here.
A uniform circular motion velocity vector changes direction; the instantaneous acceleration is inward even though the speed is constant.
science_records.units_and_signs: r in m, T in s; speed m/s; x and y east/north in m.

core1a.phenomenon: Two surveyors mark the same corridor from opposite ends; their labels differ but the physical location of each marker does not.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A coordinate is a label for position relative to a chosen origin and direction. To compare readings from different rulers, first identify shared physical markers. A uniform ruler has a constant signed scale: subtract two paired readings to cancel the offset and determine the scale. One anchor then determines the offset. This explains why a shift of origin does not change displacement and why reversing an axis reverses its signed component. The physical separation remains the absolute difference in calibrated metre coordinates. Calibration is a model: two marks alone do not establish that every intermediate mark on a damaged ruler is equally spaced. A third independent check can invalidate the assumption. This is distinct from measuring the length of the travelled path.
prerequisites: Read a number line, subtract signed numbers and convert lengths to metres.

core1a.phenomenon: A delivery robot visits recorded checkpoints, but its tracker may miss a detour between them.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A signed position change is determined by the initial and final points alone. Distance depends on the route: every piece of actual motion contributes a nonnegative length. Break a straight route at each real reversal, not just at each convenient recording time. Adding signed changes cancels intermediate positions, whereas adding their magnitudes preserves travel. The triangle inequality establishes the endpoint lower bound. If the logger records only some checkpoints, the sum of successive absolute changes is itself a lower bound; an unobserved turn can add distance without changing any sampled position. If motion is monotone between checkpoints, the bound is attained. This distinction matters when interpreting logs, inferring unknown turning positions, or testing claims about an incomplete journey.

core1a.phenomenon: A commuter can end near the starting point after a long journey: the speedometer and displacement tell different stories.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A description of motion begins with position, not the answer to a numerical formula. Mark the commuter's origin and east-positive coordinate. Each trip leg changes the position by a signed amount, but each contributes a positive path length. Average speed is the accumulated path length divided by elapsed time; average velocity is the single net position change divided by the same time. The two averages can differ even for a perfectly continuous trip, and average velocity becomes zero on a round trip. Reversing the coordinate direction reverses the velocity component without changing any physical speed. Build both numerical sums from the travel log before deciding which one the experiment measures. A graph of position versus time makes the change in direction visible, while a ledger of distances preserves how far the person actually travelled.

core1a.phenomenon: A trolley rolling west slows, stops and rolls east when a steady eastward acceleration acts.
core1a.scientific_narrative: Velocity specifies speed and direction; acceleration measures how velocity changes, not merely whether speed increases. On a fixed east-positive axis, an object with negative velocity can have positive acceleration: initially it slows, then it may reverse. Divide the signed change in velocity by elapsed time to obtain average acceleration. Only with a constant-acceleration model is this also the value throughout the interval. To determine speed change, compare the signs of instantaneous velocity and acceleration. If both have the same sign, the magnitude of velocity grows; if they have opposite signs, it shrinks. At zero velocity the sign rule needs care: the next interval determines the direction of motion. A velocity-time graph separates velocity sign (height), acceleration sign (slope) and a reversal (crossing zero).

derivation_steps.action: Write initial and final velocities on a declared axis.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The velocity change is a difference of signed components.

derivation_steps.action: Compute a_avg=(v−u)/Δt; use a constant slope only when justified.

derivation_steps.action: Check the sign of v and a on each interval, splitting at v=0.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Speed is |v|, so its change depends on both signs.

model_limits: An interval average does not imply constant acceleration.

core1a.phenomenon: A vehicle's recorded position can pause, rise or fall while time keeps increasing; the slopes tell its signed motion.
core1a.scientific_narrative: To read a motion graph, first name both axes. The height of an x–t graph is position, not speed. A horizontal x–t segment means that position is temporarily unchanged, whereas an upward slope means positive signed velocity and a downward slope means negative signed velocity. To obtain a velocity–time graph from a piecewise linear position record, compute the slope for every valid interval and place that signed velocity on the corresponding time segment. Conversely, the signed area under a velocity–time curve reconstructs each position increment, so the endpoint is independently checkable. For distance, however, the magnitudes of areas are added. Crossing the horizontal position axis does not necessarily mean the vehicle has stopped; the slope at that crossing decides velocity. Changing the coordinate origin shifts the whole x–t graph vertically without changing any velocity–time segment. This is a core representation-invariance check. A finite position table alone does not determine instantaneous slopes or hidden reversals: explicitly state linear interpolation or another valid motion model. On a straight velocity–time segment, find area using a rectangle, triangle or trapezoid; if the segment crosses zero, split at that instant for the distance ledger. For a position sketch, velocity at each instant supplies its tangent slope. This area-based construction prepares the constant-acceleration equations taught in M06.
prerequisites: PH01-M01 graph axes and scaled measurements
PH01-M03 distinction between distance and displacement

derivation_steps.action: Reconstruct total displacement from signed v×Δt areas and then independently calculate distance.

A position-axis crossing says nothing by itself about velocity direction.
A sharp velocity jump on an idealized step graph is not a real finite-acceleration process.
For smoothly changing velocity, use the actual area rather than constant-velocity rectangles.
Finite position samples alone do not specify the instantaneous velocity or exact path between samples.

core1a.phenomenon: A ball rolls up a ramp, momentarily stops, and rolls back; the same position may be visited at two distinct times.
core1a.scientific_narrative: For a constant signed acceleration, the velocity graph is a straight line. Its slope gives v=u+at. The signed area of the rectangle of height u and triangle of height at gives Δx=ut+½at², even when part of the graph lies below the axis. The trapezoid expression uses the arithmetic mean of endpoint velocities only because the graph is linear. Multiplying v−u=at by v+u and substituting the area gives v²−u²=2aΔx, without dividing by a. Squaring loses velocity sign, and a position equation can yield two legitimate times when a cart passes a point on either side of a reversal. Treat roots as candidate times until the stage domain, direction and endpoint are checked. Find total distance by splitting at any zero of velocity, not by taking the absolute value of total displacement.

derivation_steps.why_valid: Constant acceleration means the slope does not vary.

derivation_steps.action: Compute signed rectangle plus triangle area, or trapezoid area.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The integral of signed velocity is displacement.

derivation_steps.action: Multiply v−u=at by v+u and use Δx=(u+v)t/2.
derivation_steps.why_valid: This eliminates elapsed time without assuming a nonzero acceleration.

model_limits: v² relation loses sign information; recover sign from time/domain.
Displacement is not distance when velocity reverses.
Variable acceleration needs a different model or piecewise intervals.

core1a.phenomenon: Two moving observers can assign different velocities to the same object, while a mathematical encounter time may fail because the motion model changes.
core1a.scientific_narrative: The ground and a uniformly moving observer can assign different positions and velocities to the same object. In a common one-dimensional axis, x_rel=x_object−x_observer and v_rel=v_object−v_observer. These differences follow by subtracting the observer position at the same time; a constant observer velocity shifts every v–t segment by the same amount. A simultaneous separation between two objects and their meeting event are invariant under this shared translation, but an individual object's displacement and path distance need not be. For piecewise motion, build each position law from its actual boundary position and use one global clock. Solve for equality only on the interval where both laws apply. If a candidate root falls outside that interval, reject it and rebuild using the correct stage.

derivation_steps.action: Declare observer, object, axis and global time before assigning signs.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Relative position and velocity are only well-defined after fixing the measurement frame and coordinate direction.

derivation_steps.action: Subtract the observer's coordinate at the same instant: x_rel=x−x_O. For a uniformly moving observer, subtract its signed velocity from the object's velocity.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Subtracting simultaneous coordinates gives relative position, and subtracting their rates gives relative velocity.

derivation_steps.action: Translate each position segment into a signed velocity (slope) and verify by graph area.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Velocity is the rate of position change; integrating a constant signed velocity across a segment gives that segment's displacement.

derivation_steps.action: Derive the encounter time within the first valid interval and test it against the interval bounds.
derivation_steps.why_valid: An equation inherits the domain of the motion conditions from which it was constructed; an out-of-domain root is inadmissible.

derivation_steps.action: Construct the second interval's position law continuously from its boundary and re-solve the encounter.
derivation_steps.why_valid: The object's position does not jump merely because it changes speed or direction at the transition.

model_limits: Elementary constant-velocity segment equations are not correct over an interval of continuously changing velocity.
A graph's signed area gives displacement, not necessarily total distance.
Relative velocity subtraction requires consistent frames and sign conventions.
A valid equation root still requires the event to fall within that equation's physical interval.
An object's displacement and distance generally depend on the observer's motion; simultaneous separation and a shared meeting event are invariant under a common translating frame.

core1a.phenomenon: A rider on a merry-go-round has a constant speedometer reading but changes direction continuously.
core1a.scientific_narrative: A circular path differs from a straight line because direction changes even when the speed is fixed. Take a circle with radius r, centre at the origin and east/north axes. A full revolution covers circumference 2πr; dividing by the period T gives constant speed. For a fraction f of a revolution, arc length is f(2πr), but displacement is the straight vector from initial to final point. Velocity at every point is tangent, perpendicular to the radius; for counterclockwise travel the tangent turns counterclockwise as the radius does. After one complete revolution the vector displacement and average velocity are zero, though the distance and speed remain positive. The changing velocity direction means acceleration exists. To see the direction of acceleration, draw two equal-length tangent velocity arrows at neighbouring points, with their tails together. Their vector difference points approximately toward the centre at the midpoint of the short arc. As the time interval shrinks, this direction approaches the inward radius at the current point; quantitative centripetal acceleration and forces are enrichment or PH02 material, not required to solve these tasks.

derivation_steps.action: Compute the fraction of a revolution from elapsed time and period.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Constant speed around a fixed circumference makes elapsed fraction equal arc fraction.

derivation_steps.action: Find the endpoint coordinates and subtract the initial vector.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Displacement depends on endpoints, not the path.

derivation_steps.action: Divide arc length and vector displacement by elapsed time separately; identify tangent direction.
derivation_steps.why_valid: Speed and velocity encode different physical quantities.

model_limits: Whole-revolution displacement is zero but speed is not.
Average velocity is the vector displacement divided by elapsed time; not the average of speed magnitudes.
Quantitative centripetal acceleration/force is an extension; no force law is needed here.

Scale B has zero at ground x=12 m, increases west and uses 1 m per division. Construct a time-aligned table of ground positions and B readings; mark each change's direction and identify the stationary interval. Assume straight monotone motion or rest between samples.
stages.reconstruct: x=4+2A gives 2,10,10,4 m; B=12−x gives 10,2,2,8 divisions. Changes in ground x are +8,0,−6 m (east, rest, west). B changes −8,0,+6 divisions. Rest is 2–5 s. Both encode the same physical motion.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the zero, signed scale, coordinate conversion or consistency check.
stages.repair: Calibrate both axes from their zero and orientation, transform each row, compare signed changes and physical lengths.
stages.boundary_test: If B is relabelled with an east-positive axis and the same zero and spacing, reconstruct its readings.

core1b.fresh_task: A field team uses ground x east-positive. Scale P has its zero at x=−6 m and increases east by 3 m per division. A second uniform scale Q records 7 at P=2 and 1 at P=6. A rover begins at Q=4, then moves exactly 10 m west. Recover its initial ground position, final P reading and final Q reading; check both scales describe the same displacement.
core1b.protected_work: Reconcile two incomplete coordinate logs using shared markers and a physical separation constraint.

stages.predict: Predict which of P and Q increases when the rover moves west.
stages.attempt: A field team uses ground x east-positive. Scale P has its zero at x=−6 m and increases east by 3 m per division. A second uniform scale Q records 7 at P=2 and 1 at P=6. A rover begins at Q=4, then moves exactly 10 m west. Recover its initial ground position, final P reading and final Q reading; check both scales describe the same displacement.
stages.reconstruct: P=2 gives x=0; P=6 gives x=12. Q calibration k=(12−0)/(1−7)=−2 m/division; x=14−2Q. At Q=4, x=6 m. After moving west 10 m, x=−4 m; P=(−4+6)/3=2/3; Q=(14+4)/2=9. Both x changes are −10 m.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the zero, signed scale, coordinate conversion or consistency check.
stages.repair: Infer one scale from two cross-observations, use the signed displacement constraint to reconstruct the missing reading and verify it.
stages.boundary_test: If the rover instead moves 10 m east from the same start, find its final P and Q readings.

core1b.fresh_task: A warehouse tracker records x=−4 m, +5 m, +1 m at 0, 4, 9 s. No speed limit or between-sample direction is given. A supervisor claims distance must be 13 m; another claims 19 m is possible. Decide what the data determine, and construct an explicit route for each feasible claim.
core1b.protected_work: Choose the appropriate exact-distance or lower-bound model for a partially observed journey, and construct counterexamples.

stages.predict: Predict whether recording the middle position fixes the total travelled distance.
stages.attempt: A warehouse tracker records x=−4 m, +5 m, +1 m at 0, 4, 9 s. No speed limit or between-sample direction is given. A supervisor claims distance must be 13 m; another claims 19 m is possible. Decide what the data determine, and construct an explicit route for each feasible claim.
stages.reconstruct: Displacement is +5 m. Minimum distance |5−(−4)|+|1−5|=9+4=13 m, attained by −4→5→1. A route −4→8→5→1 has length 12+3+4=19 m; visit 8 before 4 s, then 5 at 4 s and 1 at 9 s. Thus 13 is a minimum, not a uniquely determined total.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the sampled versus actual route, a signed leg, a cumulative length or a feasibility condition.
stages.repair: Use checkpoint-wise triangle inequalities and show distinct feasible routes under the same data.
stages.boundary_test: If a sensor certifies monotone motion on each sampled interval, which claims survive?

core1b.fresh_task: A rail trolley starts at x=+3 m (east positive). Its odometer reads 20, 28, 28, 39, 45 m at checkpoints A–E. In the four intervals it travels west monotonically, rests, travels east monotonically, then travels west monotonically. Construct a checkpoint table of ground positions, signed changes and cumulative distance since A. Identify when it first passes x=0 and whether the end displacement equals the distance.
core1b.protected_work: Translate a direction-coded odometer log into signed position and cumulative-distance representations.

stages.predict: Predict whether the odometer can decrease when the trolley travels west.

Construct a checkpoint table of ground positions, signed changes and cumulative distance since A. Identify when it first passes x=0 and whether the end displacement equals the distance.

stages.boundary_test: If the trolley turns east instead in D–E, with the same odometer readings, revise the final position and displacement.

core1b.fresh_task: A robot starts at x=−2 m, travels east to an unknown first turning point P, then west to x=1 m, then east to x=6 m. Each leg is strictly monotone. Its total distance is 23 m. Recover P, calculate the displacement and check whether an alternative claim P=0 m could satisfy the route.
core1b.protected_work: Recover an unknown turning point by combining an exact path ledger with endpoint and reversal-order constraints.

stages.predict: Predict whether P must lie east of both the starting point and the second turn.
stages.attempt: A robot starts at x=−2 m, travels east to an unknown first turning point P, then west to x=1 m, then east to x=6 m. Each leg is strictly monotone. Its total distance is 23 m. Recover P, calculate the displacement and check whether an alternative claim P=0 m could satisfy the route.
stages.reconstruct: The first turn must exceed 1 m. D=(P+2)+(P−1)+(6−1)=2P+6=23, hence P=8.5 m. Legs 10.5,7.5,5 m total 23 m; displacement +8 m. P=0 violates the required westward leg to x=1.
stages.diagnose: Locate whether the first divergence was in the sampled versus actual route, a signed leg, a cumulative length or a feasibility condition.
stages.repair: Write the signed-order-dependent distance relation, solve for the unknown turn, then verify directions and feasibility.
stages.boundary_test: Could the same three strictly monotone legs total 8 m, with the same endpoints and second turn? Explain.

core1b.fresh_task: Two motion trackers report v=−6 m/s at t=0 and +6 m/s at t=6 s. Tracker A assumes uniform acceleration; tracker B only guarantees continuous velocity and reports its average acceleration. Decide which statements follow from both records: average acceleration, existence of a reversal, exact reversal time, and uniform acceleration. Construct a second continuous piecewise-linear v–t history with a different reversal time.
core1b.protected_work: Choose whether an interval average determines a unique reversal and speed history.

stages.predict: Predict whether the endpoint data alone determine the time at which the cart stops.
stages.attempt: Two motion trackers report v=−6 m/s at t=0 and +6 m/s at t=6 s. Tracker A assumes uniform acceleration; tracker B only guarantees continuous velocity and reports its average acceleration. Decide which statements follow from both records: average acceleration, existence of a reversal, exact reversal time, and uniform acceleration. Construct a second continuous piecewise-linear v–t history with a different reversal time.
stages.reconstruct: Both have a_avg=(6−(−6))/6=+2 m/s². Continuity implies at least one zero and a sign change, not its exact time. A has v=−6+2t, zero at 3 s. B could have v=−6 at 0, 0 at 2, +6 at 6, linear on each interval, slopes +3 and +1.5 m/s². Both satisfy endpoints; neither a unique zero time nor uniform acceleration follows for B.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use explicit alternative velocity histories with identical endpoints to test a constant-acceleration assumption.
stages.boundary_test: If B certifies constant acceleration over all 6 s, what new conclusion follows?

core1b.fresh_task: A cart has a piecewise-linear velocity graph through (t in s,v in m/s): (0,−4),(2,+2),(5,+2),(7,−2). Construct an a–t step graph and a time table showing direction and whether speed increases, decreases or is constant. Give all zero-velocity times.
core1b.protected_work: Translate a piecewise signed velocity history into acceleration and speed-change intervals.

stages.predict: Predict whether the sign of acceleration alone tells the sign of velocity.
stages.attempt: A cart has a piecewise-linear velocity graph through (t in s,v in m/s): (0,−4),(2,+2),(5,+2),(7,−2). Construct an a–t step graph and a time table showing direction and whether speed increases, decreases or is constant. Give all zero-velocity times.
stages.reconstruct: Slopes are +3 for 0–2, 0 for 2–5, −2 for 5–7 m/s². Zeros: −4+3t=0 at 4/3 s; 2−2(t−5)=0 at 6 s. West/slowing 0–4/3; east/speeding 4/3–2; east/constant 2–5; east/slowing 5–6; west/speeding 6–7. At ideal corners slope is not uniquely defined; use open intervals.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Compute segment slopes and split intervals at zero velocity to construct sign and speed labels.
stages.boundary_test: Reverse the positive axis. Reconstruct acceleration signs and say which speed-change intervals differ.

core1b.fresh_task: A trolley starts at v=−5 m/s. It accelerates at +3 m/s² until an unknown time τ, then at −1 m/s² until t=8 s. Its final velocity is +3 m/s. Recover τ, velocity at the switch and zero-velocity times within the motion; justify the speed-change intervals.
core1b.protected_work: Reconstruct two acceleration stages using an unknown switch time and a velocity condition.

stages.predict: Predict whether the final positive velocity guarantees there was no earlier reversal.
stages.attempt: A trolley starts at v=−5 m/s. It accelerates at +3 m/s² until an unknown time τ, then at −1 m/s² until t=8 s. Its final velocity is +3 m/s. Recover τ, velocity at the switch and zero-velocity times within the motion; justify the speed-change intervals.
stages.reconstruct: v(8)=−5+3τ−(8−τ)=−13+4τ=3, so τ=4 s. v(4)=7 m/s. First zero at 5/3 s; second stage remains positive (7 to 3). Speed decreases 0–5/3, increases 5/3–4, decreases 4–8. Switch lies within 0–8.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Infer switch time from the velocity ledger, then determine reversal and speed history.
stages.boundary_test: If final velocity is instead −5 m/s, recover τ and determine whether a reversal occurs.

core1b.fresh_task: A cart at x=0 has u=+12 m/s and a=−3 m/s² until t=5 s, when a controller changes its motion. A sensor at x=18 m can register crossings in this interval. Decide whether v²=u²+2aΔx alone determines the number and direction of crossings; recover all valid times and signed velocities.
core1b.protected_work: Select a signed constant-acceleration law and reject roots outside a specified physical time domain.

stages.predict: Predict whether a single position can correspond to two velocity signs under uniform acceleration.
stages.attempt: A cart at x=0 has u=+12 m/s and a=−3 m/s² until t=5 s, when a controller changes its motion. A sensor at x=18 m can register crossings in this interval. Decide whether v²=u²+2aΔx alone determines the number and direction of crossings; recover all valid times and signed velocities.
stages.reconstruct: Position law 12t−1.5t²=18 gives t²−8t+12=0, roots 2 and 6 s. Only t=2 belongs to [0,5]; v=+6 m/s. The squared law gives v²=36 and cannot select sign or time domain alone. The hypothetical second crossing would have v=−6 at 6 s if the same acceleration continued.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use the position constraint to generate roots, then verify the velocity direction and stated observation window.
stages.boundary_test: If the controller change occurs at t=7 s instead, recover the valid crossings.

core1b.fresh_task: A cart starts at x=2 m with v=−3 m/s. It accelerates at +2 m/s² for 3 s, then moves with that final velocity for 2 s. Construct labelled v–t and x–t descriptions with the turning point, switch point, final position, signed displacement and total distance.
core1b.protected_work: Translate constant-acceleration stage descriptions into a continuous v–t and x–t representation with a reversal.

stages.predict: Predict whether the position at the end of the accelerating stage must differ from its initial position.
stages.attempt: A cart starts at x=2 m with v=−3 m/s. It accelerates at +2 m/s² for 3 s, then moves with that final velocity for 2 s. Construct labelled v–t and x–t descriptions with the turning point, switch point, final position, signed displacement and total distance.
stages.reconstruct: For 0≤t≤3, v=−3+2t and x=2−3t+t². Turn at t=1.5 s, x=−0.25 m; at t=3, v=+3 and x=2 m. For 3≤t≤5, v=3 and x=2+3(t−3), final x=8 m. Signed area first stage zero, second +6 m, Δx=+6 m. D=2.25+2.25+6=10.5 m. x–t is curved then linear and continuous.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use stage boundary conditions to derive v and x functions, then verify signed areas and actual path.
stages.boundary_test: If the second stage lasts 4 s rather than 2 s, what changes in both graphs and the distance?

core1b.fresh_task: A cart moves east at x=0 with unknown u. Under constant acceleration it passes x=15 m at t=2 s and x=24 m at t=4 s, measured from its start. Find u and a, determine whether it stops by t=7 s, and give the signed displacement and distance over 0–7 s if acceleration continues.
core1b.protected_work: Recover an unknown braking acceleration from two spatial observations and enforce time and stop constraints.

stages.predict: Predict whether the smaller second two-second displacement implies eastward or westward acceleration.
stages.attempt: A cart moves east at x=0 with unknown u. Under constant acceleration it passes x=15 m at t=2 s and x=24 m at t=4 s, measured from its start. Find u and a, determine whether it stops by t=7 s, and give the signed displacement and distance over 0–7 s if acceleration continues.

stages.boundary_test: If the controller instead holds the cart at rest once it reaches zero velocity, give displacement and distance by t=7.

core1b.fresh_task: A marker on a uniform counterclockwise circular track of radius 6 m is at the east point at t=0, at the west point at t=9 s, and at the north point at t=13.5 s. Its speed is known to be between 1 and 4 m/s inclusive. Decide whether one constant speed can explain the reports; determine the period and compute distance and average velocity over the first 9 s.
core1b.protected_work: Choose arc-length versus endpoint-vector models and distinguish steady speed from steady velocity.

stages.predict: Predict whether the first east-to-west record fixes the travelled arc without the speed bound.
stages.attempt: A marker on a uniform counterclockwise circular track of radius 6 m is at the east point at t=0, at the west point at t=9 s, and at the north point at t=13.5 s. Its speed is known to be between 1 and 4 m/s inclusive. Decide whether one constant speed can explain the reports; determine the period and compute distance and average velocity over the first 9 s.
stages.reconstruct: East-to-west allows 0.5,1.5,… revolutions in 9 s. Speeds are (0.5+n)12π/9: 2π/3≈2.09 for n=0, 2π≈6.28 for n=1, so only half a lap fits. T=18 s. At 13.5 s, 0.75 lap from east counterclockwise gives south, not north; reports inconsistent. Under the first two reports, D=6π m, Δr=(−12,0) m, average velocity=(−4/3,0) m/s.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Compare two timing/position reports for possible integer lap counts and use direction data to identify a compatible model.
stages.boundary_test: If the third report instead names the south point, can all three records be consistent?

core1b.fresh_task: A runner starts at the south point of a radius-5 m circle, moving clockwise at constant speed, completing a lap in 20 s. Construct a table at t=0,5,10,15,20,25 s of position coordinates (east,north), instantaneous velocity direction and cumulative distance. Calculate the vector average velocity over t=5 to 25 s and over t=0 to 15 s.
core1b.protected_work: Translate a timed circular-motion record into positions, tangent vectors, arc lengths and average vector velocity.

stages.predict: Predict whether cumulative distance and position both repeat after a revolution.
stages.attempt: A runner starts at the south point of a radius-5 m circle, moving clockwise at constant speed, completing a lap in 20 s. Construct a table at t=0,5,10,15,20,25 s of position coordinates (east,north), instantaneous velocity direction and cumulative distance. Calculate the vector average velocity over t=5 to 25 s and over t=0 to 15 s.
stages.reconstruct: Clockwise from south: south (0,−5), west (−5,0), north (0,5), east (5,0), south, west. Tangents west,north,east,south,west,north. Cumulative arc 0, 2.5π,5π,7.5π,10π,12.5π m. From 5 to 25 s same west endpoint, average velocity zero. From 0 to15 displacement (5,5) m; average velocity (1/3,1/3) m/s.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Construct aligned tables of phase, position, tangent direction and cumulative arc; check endpoints and elapsed fractions.
stages.boundary_test: If the direction reverses to counterclockwise from the same starting point with unchanged speed, reconstruct the position and tangent sequence.

core1b.fresh_task: A cyclist follows a radius-8 m circle counterclockwise, starting at north. In 18 s the odometer adds 24π m. Determine the number of revolutions, period, endpoint, final tangent direction, and vector average velocity. A friend claims the endpoint must be north because 24π is a multiple of π; test the claim.
core1b.protected_work: Recover a period and speed from a partial-lap constraint and a measured route length, then combine vector and arc quantities.

stages.predict: Predict whether the odometer distance can tell how many revolutions were completed when radius is known.
stages.attempt: A cyclist follows a radius-8 m circle counterclockwise, starting at north. In 18 s the odometer adds 24π m. Determine the number of revolutions, period, endpoint, final tangent direction, and vector average velocity. A friend claims the endpoint must be north because 24π is a multiple of π; test the claim.
stages.reconstruct: Circumference 16π m. Distance 24π implies 1.5 laps; T=18/1.5=12 s. Starting north (0,8), half-lap remainder ends south (0,−8). At south counterclockwise tangent points east. Δr=(0,−16) m, average velocity (0,−8/9) m/s; average speed 4π/3 m/s. Claim fails because the relevant multiple is circumference, not π alone.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use circumference, integer plus fractional revolutions, time and endpoint coordinates; verify the observed tangent.
stages.boundary_test: If odometer instead adds 20π m in 18 s with unchanged radius and constant speed, recover endpoint and period.

core1b.fresh_task: A patrol robot moves east at 6 m/s for 4 s, waits for 3 s and moves west at 2 m/s for 6 s. A logger reports mean moving speed 3.6 m/s; a supervisor reports overall average speed 4 m/s by averaging 6 and 2. Decide which reports are valid for their definitions, calculate overall average speed and signed average velocity, and explain the error.
core1b.protected_work: Choose the time-weighted speed and signed-velocity model from a moving-time report and an elapsed-time report.

stages.predict: Predict whether the moving-time and full elapsed-time averages must agree.
stages.attempt: A patrol robot moves east at 6 m/s for 4 s, waits for 3 s and moves west at 2 m/s for 6 s. A logger reports mean moving speed 3.6 m/s; a supervisor reports overall average speed 4 m/s by averaging 6 and 2. Decide which reports are valid for their definitions, calculate overall average speed and signed average velocity, and explain the error.
stages.reconstruct: Distance=24+12=36 m, moving time 10 s so moving average speed=3.6 m/s (valid for moving time). Full elapsed=13 s; average speed=36/13≈2.77 m/s, average velocity=+12/13≈+0.923 m/s. The unweighted mean 4 m/s ignores unequal durations and rest.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Separate elapsed and moving time, recover signed and unsigned leg contributions, and test which report uses the requested definition.
stages.boundary_test: If the westward stage lasts 12 s instead, with all other data fixed, give both overall averages and explain the direction.

core1b.fresh_task: A tracker starts at x=−4 m and records four intervals: +6 m in 2 s, rest for 3 s, −10 m in 5 s, +3 m in 1 s. Motion is constant velocity or rest in each interval. Construct aligned x–t and cumulative distance–time graphs, find the elapsed average speed and signed average velocity, and identify when the two graphs have opposite slope signs.
core1b.protected_work: Translate a signed constant-velocity travel log into position and cumulative-distance representations.

stages.predict: Predict whether the cumulative distance graph can have negative slope.
stages.attempt: A tracker starts at x=−4 m and records four intervals: +6 m in 2 s, rest for 3 s, −10 m in 5 s, +3 m in 1 s. Motion is constant velocity or rest in each interval. Construct aligned x–t and cumulative distance–time graphs, find the elapsed average speed and signed average velocity, and identify when the two graphs have opposite slope signs.
stages.reconstruct: Times 0,2,5,10,11 s; positions −4,2,2,−8,−5 m; cumulative distances 0,6,6,16,19 m. Slopes x–t +3,0,−2,+3 m/s; distance slopes +3,0,+2,+3. Opposite signs 5–10 s. Average speed 19/11 m/s, average velocity −1/11 m/s.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use the stated initial coordinate and signed legs to construct piecewise linear position and distance graphs.
stages.boundary_test: If the coordinate origin shifts 8 m east, reconstruct x–t positions and compare both averages.

core1b.fresh_task: A courier moves east at 5 m/s for an unknown time, waits 4 s, then moves west at an unknown constant speed for 6 s. The entire trip lasts 18 s and average speed is 4 m/s. Recover the first moving time, westward speed and signed average velocity. Test whether an alternative total average speed of 2 m/s could be consistent.
core1b.protected_work: Recover an unknown moving duration and speed from a total-time, distance and displacement ledger.

stages.predict: Predict whether total average speed alone can specify the direction of the final displacement.
stages.attempt: A courier moves east at 5 m/s for an unknown time, waits 4 s, then moves west at an unknown constant speed for 6 s. The entire trip lasts 18 s and average speed is 4 m/s. Recover the first moving time, westward speed and signed average velocity. Test whether an alternative total average speed of 2 m/s could be consistent.
stages.reconstruct: East time=18−4−6=8 s, east distance 40 m. Total path=4×18=72 m; west distance=32 m, west speed=16/3 m/s. Δx=40−32=+8 m, average velocity=+4/9 m/s. Alternative average speed 2 implies path 36 m, less than the east leg alone; impossible.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Use independent signed and unsigned constraints plus a rest interval to infer the missing stage and test feasibility.
stages.boundary_test: If total average speed is 5 m/s instead, recover the westward speed and signed average velocity.

core1b.fresh_task: A tracker reports x=0 m at 0 s, x=8 m at 4 s, and x=8 m at 8 s. One display explicitly joins the points with straight segments; another shows only the samples. For each display decide whether v at t=6 s and total distance are determined. Construct an alternative path consistent with the samples and give the average velocity from 0 to 8 s.
core1b.protected_work: Select a defensible motion-graph operation and distinguish observed average velocity from unobserved instantaneous velocity.

stages.predict: Predict whether identical endpoint positions on an interval always mean rest.
stages.attempt: A tracker reports x=0 m at 0 s, x=8 m at 4 s, and x=8 m at 8 s. One display explicitly joins the points with straight segments; another shows only the samples. For each display decide whether v at t=6 s and total distance are determined. Construct an alternative path consistent with the samples and give the average velocity from 0 to 8 s.
stages.reconstruct: Straight-segment model: slopes +2 then 0 m/s, v(6)=0 and D=8 m. Samples alone permit e.g. x=10 at t=6 with linear 4–6 and 6–8 legs; v at 6 need not be uniquely defined; smooth alternatives also possible. D can be 8+2+2=12 m. All have average velocity (8−0)/8=+1 m/s. The x–t area has units m·s, not displacement.
stages.diagnose: Locate the first divergence in the model, signed quantities, representation, interval constraint or independent check; do not diagnose a misconception from the final answer alone.
stages.repair: Compare sampled positions against a specified piecewise-linear model; demonstrate why a second model can share samples.
stages.boundary_test: If a sensor independently guarantees monotone motion between each pair of samples, which quantities become determined?

core1b.fresh_task: A cart begins at x=2 m. Its velocity–time graph is a straight segment from −4 m/s at t=0 to +4 m/s at t=4 s, then stays at +4 m/s to t=6 s. Construct the acceleration–time graph, a position–time sketch with coordinates at t=0,1,2,3,4,6 s, and the cumulative distance at those times. Explain the shape and slopes of the position graph and verify the total displacement and distance. Use graph areas; no constant-acceleration position formula is needed.
core1b.protected_work: Translate a piecewise-linear velocity graph into acceleration, position and cumulative-distance representations, using signed areas rather than an unintroduced motion equation.

stages.predict: Predict whether the cart's position at t=4 equals its initial position.
stages.attempt: A cart begins at x=2 m. Its velocity–time graph is a straight segment from −4 m/s at t=0 to +4 m/s at t=4 s, then stays at +4 m/s to t=6 s. Construct the acceleration–time graph, a position–time sketch with coordinates at t=0,1,2,3,4,6 s, and the cumulative distance at those times. Explain the shape and slopes of the position graph and verify the total displacement and distance. Use graph areas; no constant-acceleration position formula is needed.
stages.reconstruct: The v–t slope is +2 m/s² for 0–4 s, then 0 for 4–6 s. Velocities at 0,1,2,3,4,6 are −4,−2,0,+2,+4,+4 m/s. Signed areas over consecutive intervals are −3,−1,+1,+3,+8 m. Positions are 2,−1,−2,−1,2,10 m. Cumulative distances are 0,3,4,5,8,16 m. x–t has increasingly positive slope until t=4, horizontal tangent at t=2, and a straight positive-slope segment afterward. Net displacement +8 m and distance 16 m. Velocity is continuous at t=4; acceleration changes there.
